subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Why the photoelectric effect shows that light comes in particles
Threshold frequency: the lowest frequency that releases electrons
Einstein's equation: work function, maximum kinetic energy and stopping potential
How electron diffraction shows that matter behaves as a wave
Calculating a particle's de Broglie wavelength from its momentum
Compton scattering as further evidence that light is made of particles
Why a scattered photon comes out with a longer wavelength
Calculating the Compton shift from the scattering angle

questions.q: A student argues: 'When the intensity of light above the threshold frequency is doubled, the photocurrent doubles. This result proves that light consists of photons.' Which evaluation of this argument is correct?
options: It is valid: a wave model cannot explain why a more intense beam releases more photoelectrons.
It is flawed: the photocurrent depends on the frequency of the light, not on its intensity.
It is flawed: a wave model also predicts that more intense light releases more photoelectrons each second.
It is flawed: the photocurrent is fixed by the potential difference across the photocell, not by the light.
optionWhy: A student who treats every photon-model result as evidence against waves picks this. A wave model does explain it: more intense light carries more energy per second. The argument uses a result that does not distinguish the models.

A student who swaps the roles of frequency and intensity picks this. Above the threshold, the photocurrent is set by the number of photons per second, which is the intensity; the frequency sets the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

A result is evidence for photons only if the wave model cannot explain it. More intense waves deliver more energy per second and would also release more electrons per second, so this result fits both models. The threshold frequency, E_max independent of intensity and the lack of delay are the results that rule out the wave model.

A student who applies Ohm's law to a photocell picks this. Once the collector is positive enough to collect every photoelectron, the current is the saturation current, set by the number of photoelectrons emitted per second, which doubles when the intensity doubles.
questions.explain: A result is evidence for photons only if the wave model cannot explain it. More intense waves deliver more energy per second and would also release more electrons per second, so this result fits both models. The threshold frequency, E_max independent of intensity and the lack of delay are the results that rule out the wave model.

questions.q: Sodium has a work function of 2.28 eV. Light from a 50 mW red laser of wavelength 650 nm, and then light from a dim violet lamp of wavelength 400 nm delivering only 0.10 mW, falls on a clean sodium surface. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Which light releases photoelectrons from the sodium?
options: Only the red light, from the 650 nm laser
Only the violet light, despite its lower power
Both the red light and the violet light
Neither the red light nor the violet light
optionWhy: A student who thinks longer-wavelength light carries more energy per photon picks this. E = hc/λ: the 650 nm photons have only 1.91 eV, below the 2.28 eV work function, while the 400 nm photons have 3.11 eV. Light releases electrons only if its wavelength is SHORTER than the threshold wavelength, here 545 nm.

Violet photon: E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸)/(400 × 10⁻⁹) = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.11 eV, more than 2.28 eV. Red photon: 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.91 eV, less than 2.28 eV. The power of the laser only sets how many red photons arrive; none of them can free an electron.

A student who thinks intense light can release electrons at any frequency picks this. The violet light does release electrons, but the red photons each carry 1.91 eV, below the 2.28 eV work function, and energy from many photons does not accumulate in an electron, however powerful the laser.

A student who compares photon energies in joules (3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) directly with 2.28 concludes that both are far too small. Converting first: the violet photons have 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ ÷ 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.11 eV, above the work function, so violet light does release electrons.
questions.explain: Violet photon: E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸)/(400 × 10⁻⁹) = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.11 eV, more than 2.28 eV. Red photon: 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.91 eV, less than 2.28 eV. The power of the laser only sets how many red photons arrive; none of them can free an electron.
questions.working: Red: E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(650 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = (3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) eV = 1.91 eV < 2.28 eV, so no emission at any power. Violet: E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)(3.00 × 10⁸)/(400 × 10⁻⁹) = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.11 eV > 2.28 eV, so photoelectrons are emitted (E_max = 3.11 − 2.28 = 0.83 eV). Equivalently, λ₀ = hc/Φ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)(3.00 × 10⁸)/(2.28 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 5.45 × 10⁻⁷ m = 545 nm; only wavelengths shorter than this release electrons.

questions.q: For each of two metals, P and Q, a student plots the maximum kinetic energy E_max of the photoelectrons against the frequency f of the incident light. Both graphs are straight lines. The line for P meets the frequency axis at 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and the line for Q meets it at 7.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Which statement about the two lines is correct?
options: Q's line is steeper, because its gradient is set by the larger work function.
Each line shows the kinetic energy of every photoelectron at that frequency.
Each line would be shifted upwards if light of greater intensity were used.
They have equal gradients, each equal to the Planck constant h.
optionWhy: A student who reads the work function from the gradient picks this. The gradient of E_max against f is h for every metal. The work function appears in the intercepts: the line meets the frequency axis at f₀ = Φ/h and, extended, meets the E_max axis at −Φ.

A student who thinks every photoelectron leaves with the same energy picks this. Each point on a line is the MAXIMUM kinetic energy, hf − Φ. Φ is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron; electrons from below the surface lose extra energy on the way out and leave with less, down to zero.

A student who thinks brighter light gives each photoelectron more energy picks this. E_max = hf − Φ contains no intensity: more intense light of the same frequency releases more electrons per second, not faster ones, so each line stays where it is.

E_max = hf − Φ has the form y = mx + c with gradient h for every metal, so the lines are parallel. They are displaced because Q has the larger work function: Φ = hf₀, so Φ_Q − Φ_P = h × 2.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
questions.explain: E_max = hf − Φ has the form y = mx + c with gradient h for every metal, so the lines are parallel. They are displaced because Q has the larger work function: Φ = hf₀, so Φ_Q − Φ_P = h × 2.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

questions.q: In an electron diffraction tube the accelerating potential difference is 3.0 kV and one of the rings on the screen has a radius of 24 mm. The accelerating potential difference is increased to 6.0 kV. Assume the electrons are non-relativistic and that the radius of the ring is proportional to the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons. What is the new radius of this ring?
options: 12 mm
34 mm
24 mm
17 mm
optionWhy: A student who uses the photon relation λ = hc/E takes λ ∝ 1/E_k and halves the radius. For a particle with mass, p = √(2mE_k), so λ ∝ 1/√E_k and the radius falls by √2, to 17 mm.
A student who thinks faster particles have longer wavelengths multiplies by √2. λ = h/p: the electrons gain momentum, so their wavelength and the ring radius DECREASE, to 24/√2 = 17 mm.

A student who thinks the ring pattern is set only by the arrangement of the atoms, as for particles deflected by them, expects no change. The ring angles depend on the electrons' de Broglie wavelength, which decreases as the potential difference increases.
E_k = eV and p = √(2m_e eV), so λ = h/p ∝ 1/√V. Doubling V divides λ, and so the radius, by √2: 24 mm/√2 = 17 mm.
questions.explain: E_k = eV and p = √(2m_e eV), so λ = h/p ∝ 1/√V. Doubling V divides λ, and so the radius, by √2: 24 mm/√2 = 17 mm.
questions.working: E_k = eV, so p = √(2m_e eV) and λ = h/√(2m_e eV) ∝ 1/√V. With r ∝ λ: r_new = r × √(V₁/V₂) = 24 mm × √(3.0 kV/6.0 kV) = 24 mm/√2 = 17 mm.

questions.q: In a scattering experiment, a beam of high-energy electrons, each of momentum 2.24 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹, is directed at a thin carbon target. The intensity of the electrons scattered by the carbon nuclei is measured at different angles to the beam, and the first minimum of intensity is found at 51°. Assume the first minimum occurs at the angle θ where sin θ ≈ λ/D, where λ is the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons and D is the diameter of a nucleus. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. What is the estimated diameter of a carbon nucleus?
optionWhy: A student who uses cos 51° = 0.629 in place of sin 51° gets 4.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. The first minimum is given by sin θ ≈ λ/D, with θ measured from the direction of the beam.
A student whose calculator is in radian mode gets sin 51 = 0.670 and D = 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. The angle is in degrees: sin 51° = 0.777.

A student who thinks diffraction happens when the wavelength equals the size of the object sets D = λ = 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. The size is found from the angle of the first minimum: D ≈ λ/sin θ = 3.8 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.

questions.q: A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg is bowled at 30 m s⁻¹ towards a gap several metres wide between two fielders. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Which statement explains why no diffraction of the ball is observed?
options: It has no de Broglie wavelength, since it is not a subatomic particle.
Its de Broglie wavelength is far too short compared with the width of the gap.
It is uncharged, and only charged particles such as electrons diffract.
Its de Broglie wavelength does not equal the gap width, and diffraction needs them equal.
optionWhy: A student who thinks only tiny particles have wave properties picks this. λ = h/p applies to any object with momentum; the ball's wavelength is 1.4 × 10⁻³⁴ m, not zero, but far too short to show diffraction.

λ = h/p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(0.16 × 30) = 1.4 × 10⁻³⁴ m. Diffraction is noticeable only when the wavelength is comparable with the gap; here it is about 10³⁴ times smaller, so the spreading is immeasurably small.

A student who thinks diffraction of particles is an electrical deflection by atoms picks this. Diffraction is a wave effect: uncharged neutrons, atoms and molecules diffract. The ball does not because its wavelength is so short.

A student who thinks diffraction happens only when the wavelength equals the gap picks this. Diffraction is noticeable whenever the wavelength is comparable with the gap, not only when the two are equal. The ball's λ = h/p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(0.16 × 30) = 1.4 × 10⁻³⁴ m, about 10³⁴ times smaller than the gap, which is why no diffraction is seen.
questions.explain: λ = h/p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(0.16 × 30) = 1.4 × 10⁻³⁴ m. Diffraction is noticeable only when the wavelength is comparable with the gap; here it is about 10³⁴ times smaller, so the spreading is immeasurably small.
questions.working: p = mv = 0.16 kg × 30 m s⁻¹ = 4.8 kg m s⁻¹. λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)/(4.8 kg m s⁻¹) = 1.4 × 10⁻³⁴ m, about 10³⁴ times smaller than a gap of a few metres.

questions.q: The photoelectric effect shows that light delivers its energy in quanta of energy hf. A student claims that Compton scattering simply confirms this and gives no additional evidence for the particle nature of light. Which statement about Compton scattering is correct?
options: It shows that a photon also carries momentum h/λ, exchanged with one electron in a collision that conserves momentum and energy.
X-rays are scattered in every direction by the electrons in the target, which a wave could not do, so the X-rays must be particles.
It shows that X-rays consist of photons, whereas the photoelectric effect shows this only for visible and ultraviolet light.
Photons must have mass, because only a particle with mass can carry momentum into a collision with an electron.
optionWhy: The photoelectric effect tests only the photon's energy. Compton's results, including the dependence of the shift on angle, are reproduced by treating the event as a two-body collision in which a photon of momentum h/λ and energy hc/λ collides with one electron and both quantities are conserved. This is additional, independent evidence that light behaves as particles.

A student who takes any particle-sounding description as evidence picks this. Waves are also scattered in all directions by electrons, so the direction of scattering distinguishes nothing. The evidence lies in the change of wavelength and its dependence on angle.

A student who thinks the photon model applies only to certain parts of the spectrum picks this. The photoelectric effect occurs with X-rays too, and the photon description applies to radiation of every frequency. The new evidence is about momentum, not about which radiation counts as photons.

A student who reasons from p = mv that momentum needs mass picks this. A photon has zero rest mass but carries momentum h/λ = E/c; Compton scattering demonstrates that this momentum is exchanged with the electron, not that photons are massive.
questions.explain: The photoelectric effect tests only the photon's energy. Compton's results, including the dependence of the shift on angle, are reproduced by treating the event as a two-body collision in which a photon of momentum h/λ and energy hc/λ collides with one electron and both quantities are conserved. This is additional, independent evidence that light behaves as particles.

questions.q: An X-ray photon of wavelength 2.20 × 10⁻¹¹ m is scattered by a free electron that is initially at rest. The scattered photon has wavelength 2.60 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the kinetic energy of the recoiling electron?
optionWhy: The photon loses energy to the electron. E_i = hc/λ_i = 9.04 × 10⁻¹⁵ J and E_f = hc/λ_f = 7.65 × 10⁻¹⁵ J, so the electron gains E_i − E_f = 1.39 × 10⁻¹⁵ J as kinetic energy.

A student who treats the event like the photoelectric effect, with the whole photon energy hc/λ_i absorbed by the electron, picks this. In Compton scattering the photon survives with energy hc/λ_f = 7.65 × 10⁻¹⁵ J, and the electron receives only the difference.

A student who substitutes the change in wavelength into E = hc/λ, giving hc/Δλ with Δλ = 4.0 × 10⁻¹² m, picks this. That is five times the incident photon's whole energy, which is impossible. E is inversely proportional to λ, so subtract the two photon energies.

A student who uses h/λ as the photon energy picks this. h/λ is the photon's momentum, so h/λ_i − h/λ_f = 4.64 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹ is a momentum, not an energy. The photon energy is hc/λ, a factor c larger.
questions.explain: The photon loses energy to the electron. E_i = hc/λ_i = 9.04 × 10⁻¹⁵ J and E_f = hc/λ_f = 7.65 × 10⁻¹⁵ J, so the electron gains E_i − E_f = 1.39 × 10⁻¹⁵ J as kinetic energy.
questions.working: Incident photon energy E_i = hc/λ_i = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(2.20 × 10⁻¹¹ m) = 9.04 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. Scattered photon energy E_f = hc/λ_f = (1.989 × 10⁻²⁵ J m)/(2.60 × 10⁻¹¹ m) = 7.65 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. Energy is conserved and the electron starts at rest, so E_k = E_i − E_f = 9.04 × 10⁻¹⁵ − 7.65 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 1.39 × 10⁻¹⁵ J (about 8.7 keV). The shift of 4.0 × 10⁻¹² m is less than the maximum Compton shift 2h/m_e c = 4.85 × 10⁻¹² m, so the data are physically possible.

questions.q: X-rays of wavelength 7.10 × 10⁻¹¹ m are Compton scattered by free electrons. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the wavelength of the X-rays scattered through an angle of 120°?
optionWhy: A student who subtracts the shift gets 7.10 × 10⁻¹¹ − 0.364 × 10⁻¹¹ = 6.74 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Δλ = λ_f − λ_i is positive: the scattered photon has less energy and a LONGER wavelength.
A student who uses cos θ in place of (1 − cos θ) gets Δλ = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² × (−0.50) = −1.21 × 10⁻¹² m and λ_f = 6.98 × 10⁻¹¹ m. The factor is 1 − cos 120° = 1.50.
A student whose calculator is in radian mode gets cos 120 = 0.814, so 1 − cos θ = 0.186 and Δλ = 4.5 × 10⁻¹³ m. In degrees, cos 120° = −0.50 and 1 − cos θ = 1.50.

questions.q: X-rays of wavelength 7.1 × 10⁻¹¹ m and visible light of wavelength 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m are each scattered through 90° by free electrons. The Compton shift is easily measured for the X-rays but not for the visible light. Take h/(m_ec) = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m. What is the reason?
options: The shift is the same for both, but it is a tiny fraction of the visible wavelength.
The shift is far smaller for visible light, as visible photons carry much less energy.
Visible light is scattered only as a wave, since just high-frequency radiation acts as photons.
Visible photons carry more energy than X-rays, so a small energy loss alters their wavelength less.
optionWhy: Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos 90°) = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m whatever the incident wavelength. It is 2.4 × 10⁻¹²/7.1 × 10⁻¹¹ ≈ 3% of the X-ray wavelength but only 2.4 × 10⁻¹²/5.0 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁶ of the visible wavelength, too small to measure.

A student who expects the shift to depend on the photon's energy picks this. The formula contains no incident wavelength: at 90° the shift is 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m for both. Only its size relative to the wavelength differs.

A student who thinks only X-rays and gamma rays are photons picks this. All electromagnetic radiation consists of photons; visible light even shows the photoelectric effect. Visible photons undergo the same shift, but it is negligible compared with their wavelength.

A student who thinks longer-wavelength photons carry more energy picks this. E = hc/λ: a 500 nm photon has about 7000 times LESS energy than a 0.071 nm X-ray photon. In fact the shift at 90°, 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m, is the same for both; it is simply a tiny fraction of the visible wavelength.
questions.explain: Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos 90°) = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m whatever the incident wavelength. It is 2.4 × 10⁻¹²/7.1 × 10⁻¹¹ ≈ 3% of the X-ray wavelength but only 2.4 × 10⁻¹²/5.0 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁶ of the visible wavelength, too small to measure.
questions.working: Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos 90°) = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m × 1 = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m for both. Fraction of X-ray wavelength: 2.4 × 10⁻¹²/7.1 × 10⁻¹¹ = 0.034 (3%). Fraction of visible wavelength: 2.4 × 10⁻¹²/5.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 4.8 × 10⁻⁶ (about 0.0005%).
